newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian rate cut hopes rise on wages.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-FOCUS-Australian rate cut hopes rise on wages.

text.p: The likelihood of an Australian interest rate cut in 1996 increased markedly on Thursday after data showed wages growth matched Wednesday's inflation performance by falling to a two-year low, economists said.

Wages were seen as the main stumbling block in the way of a rate cut, but the favourable data raised expectations that the Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) will cut rates, possibly as soon as November 6 after the next RBA board meeting.
"It is hard to overstate how good these numbers are," Bankers Trust Australia senior economist Peter Munckton said.

Average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 0.7 percent in the three months to August, taking the annual rate of wage increases down to 3.5 percent from 3.7 percent in May and 5.2 percent one year ago.

The wages news came just one day after data showed the consumer price index (CPI) had fallen to 2.1 percent, its lowest level in two years, and the key underlying inflation rate had fallen under three percent for the first time in over a year.
"If inflation numbers were a necessary condition for an easing, today's wages numbers were a sufficent condition," Commonwealth Bank chief economist Bruce Freeland said.

The RBA aims to keep underlying rate to between two and three percent over a run of years. Wages are a key influence on the underlying rate, which removes seasonal and volatile items from the CPI, so the slowing in wages was seen as a positive.
"Today's wages data were at the low end of expectations and are an unambiguously good sign for continuing low inflation," Commonwealth's Freeland said.

With inflation and wages both moderating and below what the market sees as the RBA's danger zones, the rate cut could be delivered to provide further stimulus to the economy and stalling labour market.

"The easing in quarterly growth is certainly a positive sign and yet another signal, along with decelerating inflation and high unemployment, that the fundamentals are supportive of an easing in official rates," ANZ Securities economists said.
Industry groups and politicians joined economists in calling for a rate cut after the better-than-expected combination of wages and inflation data.
"Following on from the CPI, there can be no doubt that interest rates should come down and they should come down now," Australian Chamber of Commerce and Industry chief executive Mark Paterson said.
Ahead of the data being released, Prime Minister John Howard said in a radio interview he hoped the wages data would lead to a reduction in interest rates.

Soon after the data was released Treasurer Peter Costello told reporters that "as a general principle, I'd point out that low inflation and moderate wage growth always brings its own rewards and the rewards that it brings is that it lessens pressure in relation to interest rates."
Bond and stocks rallied on the wages data.

Bonds yields fell to under 7.40 percent, their lowest levels in over 2-1/2 years while the main stock market index, the All Ordinaries index, rose more than one percent to just below its all time high of 2380.8 high posted earlier this month.
The Australian dollar, however, fell to just above US$0.7910 from above US$0.7930 on the news, as a rate cut would lessen the attractiveness of local interest rates to offshore investors.
